steps.observation: You have 900 seconds. Write a short story about a lighthouse keeper.

steps.action:
The storm hit on a Tuesday.

Elias knew it was coming long before the sky darkened. The air had changed that morning—thicker, heavy with a metallic tang that clung to the back of his throat as he climbed the narrow stair up the tower. Years alone with the sea had taught him to listen not just with his ears, but with his bones. Something in the way the waves struck the basalt base of the island left no doubt.

He paused by the lantern room’s hatch, hand resting on the worn iron handle, and listened. Far below, the Atlantic hurled itself against Graystone Rock in long, deliberate blows. Between each crash came a brief, taut silence, as if the ocean were drawing breath for worse.

“I know,” he murmured. “I hear you.’

He pushed open the hatch. The lantern room breathed out warm, oil-scented air. The great lens—four meters of bevelled glass and brass—stood in the center of the room like a frozen wave, catching the weak afternoon light and throwing it into soft rainbows on the curved walls.

The light was his life. Literally, if one counted the government stipend paid to maintain it, and in every other sense that mattered. When he had arrived seven years earlier, Graystone Light had been half-abandoned: the glass clouded with dust, the clockwork seized, the paint flaking like scabbed skin from the tower’s flank. Two other keepers had come and gone, but the isolation pressed in on them until they broke and fled back to the mainland.

Elias had stayed. He had learned Schubert’s piano pieces by memory and hummed them to the gulls. He had mapped the migration of the seals that bred on the sheltered side of the rock each autumn. He had repaired the rusted gears, polished the glass, and coaxed the light back into its rotation: a beam every twelve seconds, sweeping the horizon like a long, slow blink.

He rarely thought of the city now. On calm days, he could imagine it had drifted away like fog.

He walked a slow circle around the lantern, palm trailing along the cold brass frame, checking for hairline cracks, warped fittings, anything that might fail when wind became a solid force trying to rip the tower from the world. The great lens stared outward through the thick panes of the lantern room, a cyclopean eye waiting for dusk.

Halfway through his inspection, he caught sight of the first low bank of storm cloud: a bruise spreading along the western horizon. The line between sea and sky blurred, then vanished entirely. Even this far out, a few gulls still wheeled, but they were flying low and fast toward the lee of the rock. Sensible creatures, gulls. They knew when the world meant business.

He finished his circuit, found nothing amiss, and descended.

The stair wound down through the tower like the thread of a screw. Whitewashed stone walls curved tight around him, prickled with moisture where the wind found tiny cracks. Every few meters, a small window cut into the masonry showed him a different slice of world: darkening water, a sky thickening like boiled milk, the black teeth of the reef stretching north and south of the island.

At the base, he stepped into the keeper’s quarters: a compact set of rooms snugged up against the tower’s flank. He had arranged them the way he liked—practical, bare, and clean. A narrow bed under a porthole. A table bearing his logbooks, a kerosene lamp, and a chipped mug with a painted green stripe around the rim. Shelves lined with tins of beans and peaches, sacks of flour, coils of rope, a faded deck of cards. A small frame on the wall held a photograph: four people squinting in winter sunlight, their smiles lopsided with surprise. One of them was him, younger, less weathered. The woman beside him—Mara—tilted her head toward him as if half-expecting to hear him say something. The other two, their children, leaned in from either side, pressed into the space their parents created.

He did not look at the photograph much these days. But he had never taken it down.

The radio sat on a low table under the window, its casing scarred from years of salt air. In good weather, it crackled with distant voices: coast guard dispatches, fishing boats calling in their positions, the coastal station reading out the barometer and tide tables, the occasional burst of static-laced music. Today, as the barometer needle slid down past “Stormy,” the airwaves were busier.

“...repeat, all small craft advised to return to port—”

“—southwesterly winds increasing to force eight, backing south by nightfall—”

He tuned it until he caught the coast guard frequency. A man’s voice, calm in that particular way of people used to saying alarming things, came through the static.

“Lightstations in sectors Foxtrot through Juliet, confirm readiness. Over.”

Elias lifted the microphone, pressed the battered transmit key.

“Graystone Light, sector Hotel. Readiness confirmed. Over.”

“Copy, Graystone. Expect severe conditions from 1800 hours. Traffic heavy on your stretch tonight. Maintain full operational status and report any failures immediately. Over.”

“Understood. Graystone out.”

He set the microphone down and checked the clock above the doorway. 14:10. Four hours until storm onset. Two hours until sunset. He had time to make a pot of soup, check the fuel lines, run a hand lamp and spare chimney up to the watch room, double-secure the shutters on the lower windows. He had done this a hundred times, maybe more.

He moved through the checklist with steady efficiency. This, at least, was simple: things to tighten, things to fill, things to stow so they would not become shrapnel when the tower shook. The wind rose by degrees, fingernails of air becoming hands, hands becoming shoulders, shouldering the tower with growing insistence.

By the time he lit the big kerosene stove and hung the soup pot from its hook, rain had begun to drum on the windows in a fast, dense patter. He looked out through runnels of water just long enough to see the ocean froth with whitecaps, lines of them marching toward the island in tight ranks.

On the wall near the window hung a map: the lighthouse’s sector traced out in pencil arcs, bearing numbers scrawled in his own hand. Shoal. Safe depth. Rock. Wreck. In the years he’d been there, three ships had gone down on those rocks. One had tried to cut too close in fog to save an hour. One had lost her engines in a winter gale. One had burned, the fire a sickly orange smear against the night, until the wind drove her into the reef like a hammer on glass.

The light had been burning each time, its beam sweeping in its patient pattern. He had watched from the gallery as men clung to upturned hulls and fragments of deck. He’d flung lines into waves no rope could bite. The sea had given back some of them, coughing them up on the slipperiest stones, blue and silent. The rest were down in the cold dark, among the torn steel and the slow, waving scraps of net.

He tended his pot and did not think of them. The keeper’s work was not to carry the lost. Only to stand watch for the living.

At 16:12, he climbed the stair again, lantern in hand. Outside, the storm had become a roar, a constant battering presence that turned the tower into the hollow of a drum. Each gust made the wall lean a fraction, a bending he felt as a subtle shift in his balance. He kept one hand on the inner rail, feeling the vibrations through the iron. The air up here smelled sharper, streaked with the iodine breath of the sea.

At the watch room just below the lantern, he set the hand lamp on the small table beside the log and wrote the hour in firm strokes.

16:12 – Barometer 28.4 and falling. Wind SW, force 7, increasing. Visibility moderate, rain. Lit main lamp.

He climbed the last few steps to the lantern room.

The world beyond the glass had become an indistinct churn of gray: air and water blurred together, the line between them lost. In the near field, he could make out the smaller waves shouldering each other, their tops ripped away by the wind in white streamers. Beyond that, nothing. The horizon might as well have been the edge of existence.

He moved with careful, habitual motions. Checked the fuel level in the lamp’s reservoir. Pivoted one of the panels of the lens aside and lit the mantle with his hand lighter, shielding the flame with his body until it caught. For a moment, the wick smoldered, smelling of scorched fabric. Then, with a soft, almost apologetic whoof, the mantle flared to life.

He opened the panel again and watched the light expand within the lens, caught, focused, and hurled outward as the rotation gearbox began its slow, steady turn. Outside, a spear of yellow-white cut into the darkening storm, swept the unseen sea in its twelve-second arc, vanished, and returned.

The first time he’d lit the restored lamp years ago, he had felt an unexpected emotion—something like awe, or relief. A human-made thing, insisting on presence in a landscape that chewed iron and bone without distinction. He felt a muted echo of it now.

He stood for a while, watching the beam walk the hurricane wall of rain. He could not see beyond a quarter-mile, maybe less, but out there, somewhere within this circle of influence, were hulls and men whose only knowledge of him would be that, tonight, the light was burning.

He descended to the watch room and settled into the high-backed wooden chair by the small, rain-streaked window. On the table, the log lay open. Beside it sat the black metal box of the radio’s remote head, speaker humming softly, occasional bursts of chatter rising and falling beneath the wash of static and wind.

For a time, he just listened.

“—trawler Asterion south-southwest of Graystone, reducing speed—”

“—copy, Asterion, maintain at least three miles off Graystone reef, repeat, three miles off—”

“—bulk carrier Orpheus, altering course twenty degrees starboard to avoid weather system—”

He noted each ship that reported within his sector, pencil moving steadily. It was not strictly required anymore; the coast guard kept digital logs now. But the act of writing anchored him.

On the next sweep of the beam, something flickered in the corner of his eye. He leaned toward the window.

There. Through the blur of rain, in that brief interval where the beam grazed the southeast, he thought he saw a light: small, low to the water, bouncing with too-quick irregularity. Not the measured blink of a buoy or the steady glow of a ship’s masthead.

He waited, counting under his breath. Twelve seconds. The beam returned, slid over the water—

Yes. Clearer, this time. A white point, jostled, then half-obscured by spindrift.

He rose, heart knocking once against his ribs with the sure, hollow sound of a struck bell. He reached for the binoculars that hung from a hook above the table and swept them up, cold against his face.

It took a few passes before he found it, his hands compensating for the swing of the tower and the roll of the sea. But the lens caught it finally: a small vessel, no more than eight or nine meters, nose up, stern fighting the waves. A cabin cruiser, by the look of her—pleasure craft, not meant for this kind of weather. Her running lights bobbed like fireflies on a storm-tossed pond.

He saw, as the next wave lifted her, that she was far too close.

Even without his annotated charts, he knew that patch of water by feel. The reef there rose in jagged spires, some just beneath the surface. In weather like this, they would be invisible until the last second. Or until they ripped the hull out from under you.

He did not think. He set the binoculars down—too hard, the rubber casing thumped on the table—and grabbed the microphone.

“Unidentified small craft in the vicinity of Graystone Light, this is Graystone Lightstation. You are approaching dangerous shoals. Alter course north by northeast immediately. Do you read? Over.”

Static answered him, long and sibilant, like the sea drawn across pebbles.

Again. “Unidentified small craft near Graystone, you are standing into danger. Alter course north by northeast. Acknowledge. Over.”

The speaker spit and hissed. Then, under the crackle, a voice broke through, thin and frayed.

“—Graystone, this is—it’s the Merrilee. Engine…engine’s quitting on us. We’re trying to hold—” A blast of interference swallowed the rest. Then: “—not answering helm, we’re—Jesus—”

Elias pressed the transmit key almost before the sentence ended. “Merrilee, this is Graystone. You are in a hazardous area. Can you steer at all? Over.”

“—maybe—a little. We lost main power ten minutes ago. Running on battery and what’s left of the engine. We can’t make headway. The waves…” The word dissolved in a sound that might have been laughter or a sob. “We can see your light. Feels like we’re not getting any closer. Over.”

He closed his eyes for a fraction of a second, seeing it: their bow tipping up and down, every surge stealing more control, every trough nudging them where they could not afford to go.

“How many souls aboard, Merrilee? Over.”

A pause. The voice that came back was higher, someone else. A woman. “Two,” she said. “Just two.”

Behind her, faintly, a child cried.

Elias opened his eyes. The room seemed to tighten around him. “Correction received,” he said, voice steady only through long practice. “Two adults and one child, is that right? Over.”

“Yes. She’s eight.” The woman’s voice shook on the last word. “Please. We—we thought we had time to beat the storm in. The forecast said it would hold off and then the engine—” Words tumbled over each other, jammed by fear.

“Listen,” Elias said. “Listen to me now.”

He did not say over. The old radio protocol frayed when fear entered the circuit. But some habits were too deep to break; after a heartbeat, she murmured, “Listening. Over.”

He let out a breath he had not realized he’d been holding. “You are three-quarters of a mile southeast of Graystone, heading toward a reef. You must turn your bow into the wind and hold it there as best you can. Do not try to come closer to the island on this heading. Do you understand? Over.”

“We’re trying. The wheel—” static “—keeps jerking. It doesn’t…” More interference.

He glanced at the barometer on the wall. 28.1. The needle was nearly on the peg. Outside, the storm had found its full voice. The tower shook in earnest now, a slow, deep vibration like a growled warning.

He remembered another storm, another voice on the radio.

Mara, in their little apartment above the fishmonger’s on Harbor Street. The phone clamped between shoulder and ear while he signed the first set of papers for the transfer to Graystone. Her silence stretching down the line like a taut rope.

“So,” she had said after a long moment, “you’re really going to do this.”

“It’s only for a year,” he had said. “They need someone to get the place in order, that’s all. After that, we’ll see.”

“We’ve been ‘seeing’ for a long time, Eli.”

The sea had always called louder than anything else. He had grown up with its mutter in his ears, its smell in his clothes. He had signed on to crewing ships before he was old enough to drink, following the coast from one end of the country to the other and beyond, always promising he would come home for good after the next run, after the next contract. Mara had waited, raised the kids, kept the little apartment warm as she could.

When the offer from Graystone came—steady pay, work that mattered, a chance to be with the sea without leaving land beneath his feet—it had seemed like an answer. But it had been another departure, just in slower motion.

“Dad,” their son had said, twelve and long-limbed, when they came out to see the station for the first and only time. “It’s like you live on the moon.”

He had ruffled his hair. “A very small, wet moon,” he’d said, and tried to make it a joke.

The visits had thinned as the months turned into years. The lighthouse was a long trip and a rough one in winter; school and work filled their days. Phone calls did not like the thick stone walls. Messages took time to reach. In between storms and repairs and night watches, he told himself he would go back for a good, long stay soon.

But the sea kept breaking itself against Graystone, and the light kept needing tending.

“Merrilee, this is Graystone,” he said now. The child was still crying in the background, a high, keening sound that wormed under the storm’s roar. “I’m going to coordinate with the coast guard. Stay with me on this frequency. Keep your bow to the wind. If you have any anchor, drop it now. It may catch on something, slow you. Over.”

“We don’t—” another burst of static “—we have a small one. For the bay. Will it—”

“It’s better than nothing,” he said. “Get it overboard. Make sure the line is secured. Over.”

He could picture it: some small recreational anchor, meant for sand and mud, not the torn, jagged bottom near Graystone. It might snag a crevice. It might not. But giving them action, something concrete to do, might fight the paralysis gathering like ice in their limbs.

He switched frequencies, thumb moving with memory’s sureness.

“Coast Guard Station Halloway, this is Graystone Lightstation. Distress situation in my sector. Over.”

It took ten seconds—a long time now—for the reply. “Graystone, Halloway. Go ahead. Over.”

“Small craft Merrilee, eight- to nine-meter cabin cruiser, three souls aboard, engine failing. Current position approximately three-quarters mile southeast of my station, drifting onto the south reef. Conditions severe. Request immediate assistance. Over.”

Static, then: “Copy distress, Graystone. We’re tracking the storm as well. Deploying rescue vessel now is…” The voice hesitated for the first time. “Risky. Over.”

He looked at the clock. 16:47.

“How long?” he said. “Over.”

“Fastest we can do, with this sea, is forty-five minutes, maybe an hour for the cutter to reach your vicinity. And that’s an estimate, not a promise. Over.”
